analysis.one_liner: Gives drugmakers six extra months of market exclusivity when an approved drug wins a new rare-disease use.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have added six months of market exclusivity for drugs approved for new rare-disease uses, died in the House Energy and Commerce Committee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the Secretary of Health and Human Services to add six months to a drug's exclusivity period whenever the FDA approved that drug for a new use against a rare disease [S2]. Exclusivity is the stretch of time when generic competitors are legally barred from selling copies, so the extension would have let brand-name drugmakers charge monopoly prices an extra six months per qualifying approval [S3]. The extension would have stacked on top of other exclusivity bonuses, such as those for pediatric studies and infectious-disease products [S3]. The bill included a public list of extended products, a one-year notice before a company stops making a drug, and a revocation penalty for applications containing false statements [S2]. It died in the House Energy and Commerce Committee without a vote [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the main beneficiaries would be brand-name drug manufacturers, which would gain an automatic six-month monopoly extension on a product each time it won FDA approval for a rare-disease use — delay revenue that applies to the whole medicine, not just rare-disease patients [S2][S3]. Patients with rare conditions could benefit indirectly, if the promise of extra exclusivity persuades companies to test existing drugs against rare diseases that currently have no treatment [S2].

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act to require HHS to extend a drug's exclusivity period by six months when the FDA approves that drug for a new rare-disease use [S2][S3].
It extends not only the base exclusivity periods but also, where a patent certification is involved, the period blocking generic approval — pushing generic entry six months past patent expiry [S3].

Supporters' rationale is that rewarding rare-disease repurposing gives companies a financial reason to study existing medicines for the roughly 7,000 rare diseases that often have no treatment at all.

The bill includes modest public-interest guardrails: the extension can be revoked if the application contained an untrue material statement, sponsors must give one year's notice before discontinuing production, and the public must be notified of which products receive extensions [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: The cost would fall on patients, insurers, and employers who pay for the affected drugs: every six-month extension delays generic and biosimilar competition and keeps prices higher, for everyone who takes the medicine, including people taking it for common conditions [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Patients and insurers paying drug prices

drawbacks.text: Every six months of added exclusivity delays cheaper generic and biosimilar competition, raising costs for patients, insurers, and taxpayers for the entire population that takes the drug, not just rare-disease patients.

The extension stacks on top of other exclusivity bonuses: the bill expressly makes it 'in addition to' pediatric and qualified infectious disease product extensions, compounding how long a medicine stays monopoly-priced [S3].
The bill rewards companies for studying drugs they already sell, so the incentive to find new rare-disease uses may be small relative to the added monopoly time granted on the whole product.

The enforcement backstop is thin: the only stated ground for revoking an extension is an untrue material statement in the application, leaving little recourse if a company wins the bonus but does not deliver meaningful patient benefit [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The upside for patients is real but modest: because the bill only rewarded studying drugs that were already approved, the six-month bonus was a comparatively cheap way to nudge companies toward rare-disease uses. But the cost is broad and certain — every qualifying approval would have delayed generic and biosimilar competition across an entire medicine, stacking on top of pediatric and infectious-disease extensions [S2][S3]. Given how much of the incentive for rare-disease work already exists under current orphan-drug law, the bill tilted toward extending drugmakers' monopoly revenue more than toward new cures.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Health Subcommittee in November 2014, and no committee or floor vote ever happened before the Congress ended in January 2015 [S1][S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Gus Bilirakis introduced the bill on November 20, 2014, with three cosponsors: Reps. Butterfield, McCaul, and Hastings [S1][S3][S4].
It was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day, and to the Subcommittee on Health the next day [S5].
The only further action was the sponsor's introductory remarks in the Congressional Record on December 10, 2014 [S5].
No markup, vote, or floor action followed, and the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015, killing the bill [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Patients, insurers, and employers who buy prescription drugs are spared the six-month monopoly extensions the bill would have created, and generic manufacturers keep the market-access timeline it would have delayed. Brand-name drugmakers and the bill's sponsors did not get the added exclusivity, and rare-disease patients did not get whatever extra repurposing research the incentive might have prompted.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Patients and payers who buy drugs

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan — a Republican sponsor joined by three Democratic cosponsors and one Republican [S4] — but the bill never advanced far enough for any vote that would reveal a partisan split.

industries.note: The bill would have handed these companies an automatic six-month extension of market exclusivity each time an approved drug won a new rare-disease indication, delaying generic and biosimilar competition on the whole product. Because the bonus stacked on top of pediatric and infectious-disease extensions, it could have extended monopoly pricing on widely used medicines far beyond rare-disease patients.
Each six-month extension would have pushed back the date these companies could sell lower-cost copies of a medicine, keeping cheaper versions off the market longer.

Patient groups generally back incentives for orphan-drug development, since rare diseases often have no treatment; the bill offered a financial carrot for companies to test existing drugs against rare diseases. But the same mechanism raises prices for patients on the drugs that qualify.
